Time Series is a series of values organized by time [Ch. 5]. It involves recording events over time, whether regularly or sporadically [Ch. 5]. Time-series databases are optimized for handling such data, especially in scenarios involving high-velocity data volumes from IoT, event logs, and other use cases [Ch. 5]. Measurement data in time series is generated regularly, such as from temperature or air-quality sensors, while event-based data is irregular, created every time an event occurs, like a motion sensor detecting movement [Ch. 5]. The schema for a time series typically includes a timestamp and a few fields, making it suitable for operational analytics but not ideal for BI use cases [Ch. 5].

Micro-batch is a method of applying batch-oriented frameworks in a streaming situation, where a batch might run every two minutes to every second [Ch. 8]. It allows for batch processing with potentially lower overhead than true streaming systems, and can be suitable for use cases where the acceptable latency is higher than that required for true streaming [Ch. 8].

These batches can run from every two minutes to every second [Ch. 8]. It is often used when a team has expertise in batch-oriented frameworks like Apache Spark, allowing for quick implementation [Ch. 8]. The choice between micro-batch and true streaming depends on the use case, performance requirements, and acceptable latency [Ch. 8]. Streaming data processing involves handling data in real-time, as it is generated, rather than in batches. This approach is more complex than batch processing and requires sophisticated tools and paradigms [Ch. 2]. For instance, engineers must write code to apply various windowing methods to calculate metrics in real time [Ch. 2]. Streaming systems are crucial for serving data for analytics and machine learning, combining aspects of OLAP databases with stream-processing systems [Ch. 9]. They enable dynamic enrichment of data streams, such as adding metadata to IoT events [Ch. 8]. As streaming technologies evolve, they will become more prevalent, complementing traditional batch processing for tasks like model training and quarterly reporting [Ch. 11].

Batch vs streaming refers to two different approaches to data processing. Batch processing involves ingesting and processing data in large chunks, typically on a predetermined schedule or when a certain data size is reached [Ch. 2]. Streaming ingestion, on the other hand, processes data in a continuous, real-time fashion, making it available to downstream systems almost immediately after it is produced [Ch. 2]. Batch processing is popular for tasks like model training and weekly reporting, while streaming is favored for real-time applications where data timeliness is crucial [Ch. 2]. Both approaches can coexist in the same system, with frameworks like Flink and Spark supporting both batch and micro-batch ingestion [Ch. 3]. Micro-batching is a way to apply batch-oriented frameworks in a streaming context, with micro-batches running from every two minutes to every second [Ch. 8].
Asked as: "What is batch vs streaming?"

Column-oriented and row-oriented storage refer to different ways of organizing data in a database. In row-oriented storage, data is organized by row, as seen in CSV format [Ch. app01], while in column-oriented storage, data is organized by column, with each column stored in its own set of files [Ch. app01]. Columnar storage allows for reading only a subset of fields, which can reduce the amount of data scanned for queries, making it more efficient for analytics applications [Ch. app01, Ch. 8]. Row-oriented databases are better suited for transactional use cases, where individual rows need to be accessed quickly, while column-oriented databases excel in scenarios where large quantities of data need to be scanned, such as complex data transformations or aggregations [Ch. 6].

Data pipelines work by moving data through the stages of the data engineering lifecycle, from source systems to data warehouses or data lakes [Ch. 7]. They are designed to process data in batches or streams, and are crucial for reliable data management [Ch. 7]. Data pipelines can be traditional ETL systems or more complex setups involving multiple data sources, transformations, and model deployments [Ch. 7]. They are often implemented using pipelines as code, where data tasks and dependencies are declared in code, typically Python, and interpreted by an orchestration engine [Ch. 2]. While batch processing is common, streaming pipelines are becoming increasingly important for real-time data applications [Ch. 11].
